outcome: Theophilus Agama's May 2025 preprint introduces a new class of 'closed addition chains' and proves that all 'complete numbers' for which these chains are optimal satisfy the Scholz inequality ι(2^n-1) ≤ n-1+ι(n), extending (by a new, differently-characterized class) the set of integers for which the conjecture is known to hold; separately, Amadou Tall's paper (posted to arXiv Oct 2022, published in the peer-reviewed journal INTEGERS 24A in May 2024) proved the conjecture for an infinite family of integers with v(n)=7 and ℓ(2n)=ℓ(n) — the first known result for v(n)=7 — but that proof's first public written argument predates the 26 Jan 2024 window. The general conjecture remains open.
summary: The triage record pointed to arXiv:2504.07332 ('On the minimal length of addition chains') as an April 2025 paper proving the Scholz inequality for a new class of numbers. On direct inspection this was a triage error: 2504.07332 is by De Koninck, Doyon and Verreault, is about a counting function F(m,r) for addition-chain lengths extending a classical Erdős-type asymptotic result, and does not mention the Scholz or Scholz-Brauer conjecture at all. The actual paper matching the triage's description is Theophilus Agama's 'A note on closed addition chains and complete numbers' (Cryptology ePrint 2025/833, received 9 May 2025), which defines a new class of addition chains and proves that the (newly defined) 'complete numbers' for which these chains are optimal satisfy ι(2^n-1) ≤ n-1+ι(n). This is a genuine case of the problem as stated (a restriction to a specific class of n), so it counts as `partial` under §3.1, with `resolution_direction` confirmed (the inequality was shown to hold, not violated). Separately, I found Amadou Tall's paper proving the conjecture for an infinite family with v(n)=7 and ℓ(2n)=ℓ(n) (the first result for v(n)=7, closing a previously-open case per the paper's own account: 'There are no specific results on integers with v(n) = 7'). This paper's arXiv preprint (2210.13812) was posted 25 October 2022 and its INTEGERS journal publication came out 27 May 2024 (accepted 15 Dec 2023). Per §6.3 (date by first public written argument, never by journal publication lag), this event predates the 26 Jan 2024 frozen-revision date and is recorded here for context only, not counted as a change in the window. A long-running preprint by Theophilus Agama, 'On addition chains and progress on the Scholz conjecture' (arXiv:2108.07720, v1 Aug 2021 through v12 March 2026), gives a conditional improved upper bound on ι(2^n-1) contingent on a 'carry degree' condition that is not shown to hold for any specific n in the versions I could inspect; it remains an unpublished, much-revised preprint (12 versions over 4.5 years) and I could not confirm it establishes an unconditional new case, so I have not counted it as a separate event. No AI system of any kind — generative, formal, or otherwise — is mentioned in connection with any of these results; all are conventional hand-constructed combinatorial proofs. A February 2026 GitHub issue in the google-deepmind/formal-conjectures repository merely proposes the Scholz conjecture as a candidate for Lean formalization ('good first issue', formalizability 2/5); it records no mathematical progress and is not itself a research event.
competing_reading: One could argue the Tall v(n)=7 result should be dated to its journal publication (27 May 2024, inside the window) rather than its 2022 preprint, since INTEGERS is a peer-reviewed venue and the acceptance/refereeing process is itself part of 'what happened' to the mathematics. Under that reading this problem would show two `partial` events within the window (Tall 2024 publication + Agama 2025 preprint) rather than one. I did not adopt this reading because §6.3 explicitly instructs dating by first public written argument and explicitly warns against journal-publication lag, and the mathematical content of Tall's result was already public and available for scrutiny in Oct 2022.
what_would_settle_it: Whether any arXiv version of Agama's 2108.07720 conditional bound has been shown to apply unconditionally to an explicit infinite family of n (which would be a further `partial` event, datable to whichever version first made that claim) would clarify whether more should be counted here; reading the full v12 PDF's proof section (not just the abstract) would settle this.
